Topic 01 — Allied Health Team
Rehab Principles & Team
Protect
Principle 1
  • Healing tissue must not be overstressed.
Criteria to progress
Principle 2
  • Specific criteria to progress phase → phase.
Evidence-based
Principle 3
  • Program based on current clinical + scientific research.
Individualize
Principle 4
  • Adapt to each athlete's requirements + goals.
Team-oriented
Principle 5
  • All members → common goal: unrestricted competition, quickly + safely.
Team Physician
Role
  • MD/DO; proficient in musculoskeletal + sport-related conditions.
  • Pre-participation exams, on-field emergency care, diagnosis, referrals, medications.
Limit
  • Not daily rehab — makes final return-to-competition call.
Athletic Trainer (ATC)
Role
  • BOC-certified; works under physician supervision.
  • Daily health: prevention (tape/braces), evaluation, therapeutic exercise/modalities.
Key link
  • Team administrator: coach ↔ athlete ↔ team.
Physical Therapist
Role
  • Reduces pain, restores function; treatment strategies/long-term rehab.
  • Board-certified: SCS (sports) / OCS (orthopedic) via ABPTS.
Note
  • Often dual role with ATC for acute injuries.
S&C Professional
Role
  • Strength/power/performance focus; ideally CSCS.
  • With ATC/PT: resistance, plyometric, aerobic reconditioning → ready athlete for return.
Edge
  • Biomechanics knowledge → exercises for advanced rehab.
Exercise Physiologist
Role
  • Exercise-science background.
  • Designs conditioning around metabolic response to exercise.
Nutritionist / RD
Role
  • Food-choice guidelines → optimize tissue recovery.
  • RD: recognized by Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.
Counselor / Psychologist / Psychiatrist
Role
  • Sport background.
  • Coping strategies for mental stress of injury.
All members
Shared duty
  • Educate coaches/athletes on risks, precautions, treatments.
  • Prevent + rehabilitate injury.
Who hears first
Athlete
  • Most contact with coaches, ATC, S&C.
Risk
  • Injury often disclosed to coach/S&C before ATC → consistent communication imperative.
Weekly team meeting
Forum
  • Training requirements + restrictions per athlete.
Ask
  • Participation status? Current activities?
  • Restrictions? Progressing? Program changes?
Indication
Definition
  • Form of treatment required by athlete.
Example
  • Outfielder + shoulder impingement → maintain lower-body function.
Contraindication
Definition
  • Activity inadvisable/prohibited due to injury.
Example
  • Anterior shoulder dislocation → bench press ✗ (vulnerable anterior instability).
Tools
Two forms
  • Referral form: indications/contraindications.
  • S&C summary form: activities + athlete's subjective/objective responses.
Case: left ACL reconstruction
Context
  • Football midfielder.
  • Written by ATC, read by S&C.
Indications
Do
  • Stationary bike: progress gradually ≤ 60 min; no running.
  • Single-leg hip sled: < 90° knee flexion; start without resistance.
  • Upper-extremity resistance exercises.
Contraindications
Don't
  • Leg extension.
  • Full squats.
  • Plyometrics.
  • Running.

Topic 02 — Types of Injury
Types of Injury
Two mechanisms
Core idea
  • Injuries differ by how load is delivered.
Macrotrauma
Mechanism
  • Specific, sudden overload episode.
Microtrauma / overuse
Mechanism
  • Repeated abnormal stress, too little recovery.
Fracture (bone)
Cause
  • Direct blow → disrupted bone.
Classes
  • Closed / open / avulsed / incomplete.
Joint trauma
Dislocation
  • Complete displacement of joint surfaces.
Subluxation
  • Partial displacement → laxity/instability.
Sprain (ligament)
Grades
  • 1°: partial tear, no ↑ instability.
  • 2°: partial tear, minor instability.
  • 3°: complete tear, full instability.
Contusion
Cause
  • Direct trauma.
Effect
  • Blood/fluid accumulation around muscle; may severely limit function.
Strain
Cause
  • Indirect; muscle fiber tear.
Grades
  • 1°: partial; strong but painful.
  • 2°: partial; weak, painful.
  • 3°: complete; very weak, painless.
Tendon rupture
Cause
  • Tensile load > limit.
Failure site
  • Tendon collagen > muscle strength → failure at belly, musculotendinous junction, or bone attachment.
What it is
Definition
  • Repeated, abnormal stress.
  • Continuous training / too little recovery.
Common causes
Causes
  • Training errors (poor design, excess volume).
  • Hard/uneven surfaces; faulty technique/biomechanics.
  • ↓ motor control, ↓ flexibility, skeletal malalignment.
Training implication
Takeaway
  • Overuse = fixable cause → find and correct it.
Stress fracture
Facts
  • Most common overuse injury of bone.
  • Rapid ↑ volume or hard surfaces.
Tendinitis
Facts
  • Inflamed tendon.
  • Uncorrected cause → chronic tendinitis/tendinopathy.
Suffix
  • -itis = inflammatory condition (tendinitis, arthritis).
Tendinopathy
Facts
  • Degenerative: minimal inflammation.
  • Tendon cell damage/death + neovascularization.

Topic 03 — Tissue Healing
Three Phases of Healing
Continuum
Core idea
  • Inflammation → repair → remodeling.
  • Phases overlap along a continuum.
Inflammatory
Timing
  • ≈ 72 h.
Fibroblastic
Timing
  • From ≈ 72 h, up to ≈ 2 months.
Maturation
Timing
  • Weeks → months/years.
What it is
Definition
  • Initial reaction to injury; necessary for healing.
  • Local + systemic: red, swollen, painful; ↓ function.
How it works
Sequence
  • Hypoxia → tissue death → histamine + bradykinin → ↑ blood flow + permeability → edema.
  • Macrophages: phagocytosis of debris.
  • Platelets + macrophages → growth factors; fibroblasts migrate in.
Implication
Edema
  • ↑ joint pressure → inhibits motor neurons → weakness/atrophy.
Duration
  • ≈ 72 h; longer if poor blood supply/severe damage.
  • Prolonged → later phases delayed.
What it is
Definition
  • Repair begins (a.k.a. proliferative phase).
  • Catabolism + replacement of nonviable tissue.
  • ↑ collagen production, disorganized.
How it works
Sequence
  • Growth factors → fibroblasts synthesize type III collagen, randomly deposited.
  • New capillaries + scar tissue = framework.
  • Fibers strongest parallel to stress; many lie transverse.
Implication
Duration
  • Starts ≈ 72 h; lasts up to 2 months.
Caution
  • New tissue weaker than original → strength not yet optimal → protect it.
What it is
Definition
  • Weak repair tissue strengthened; overlaps repair phase.
  • Can begin within a few weeks of injury.
How it works
Sequence
  • Type III → stronger type I collagen.
  • Loading → collagen fibers hypertrophy + align along lines of stress.
Implication
Duration
  • Remodeling: months → years.
Result
  • Thicker, aligned fibers → return to function; still weaker than normal healthy tissue.
Athlete factors
Shift timing within each phase
  • Age.
  • Lifestyle.
  • Degree of injury.
  • Comorbidities.
Structure
Tissue type
  • Tissue type damaged changes timing.
No fixed timelines
Key idea
  • No definitive timelines.
  • All tissues follow the same basic pattern.

Topic 04 — Goals by Healing Phase
Goals by Healing Phase
Don't overstress
Rule 1
  • Controlled therapeutic stress → optimizes collagen matrix formation.
  • Too much damages new structures; too little doesn't help.
Choose load by
  • Phase, athlete type, plane of movement.
Meet criteria to progress
Rule 2
  • Objectives: ROM, strength, activity.
  • Set by team physician/ATC/PT.
Example: MCL
Why
  • Valgus (frontal-plane) stress peaks in terminal knee extension.
So
  • Avoid lateral box jump/side shuffle early; include in later phases.
Treatment goal
Goal
  • Prevent disruption of new tissue + prolonged inflammation.
  • Relative rest + physical agents (ice, compression, elevation, e-stim); efficacy mixed.
Exercise strategy
Strategy
  • Protective loading (active rest); no painful/intense work stressing the injury.
Maintain
  • Power/strength/endurance: uninjured limbs, general aerobic/anaerobic, joints proximal/distal if not stressing injury.
POLICE
Replaces PRICE
  • Protection · Optimal Loading · Ice · Compression · Elevation.
Case for
Pros
  • ↓ pain via ↓ nerve conduction velocity.
  • Suppresses inflammation → ↓ swelling, ↑ return to sport.
  • Part of POLICE in acute stage.
Case against
Cons
  • Vasoconstriction concern: largely unsupported; no evidence icing alone impedes healing.
  • After exercise: ↓ DOMS but ↓ IGF + protein synthesis → routine use not recommended.
Dosing
How
  • 15 min (ice pack/massage/cold-water immersion).
  • Immersion < 59 °F (< 15 °C) for larger areas (hand/ankle).
  • No local cryotherapy beyond acute phase.
Treatment goal
Goal
  • Prevent excessive atrophy + joint deterioration.
  • Protect weak collagen but gradually add low-load stress → ↑ synthesis, keep ROM.
Too little
  • Misaligned fibers, adhesions → ↓ motion.
Exercise strategy
Strategy
  • Avoid active resistive work of damaged tissue; submaximal: functional movement vs gravity/isometrics.
  • Ultrasound/e-stim/ice continue. Train uninjured areas + cardiorespiratory.
Timeline
Duration
  • Repair can take up to 8 weeks — longer if too much or too little stress.
Caution
  • Use only after consulting physician/ATC/PT.
Isometric
What
  • Pain-free, submaximal → keeps neuromuscular function, ↑ strength without disrupting collagen.
Limit
  • Joint-angle specific → use multiple angles.
Isokinetic
What
  • Fixed speed (60°/s, 120°/s); mostly single-joint.
  • Early/post-op continuous passive motion; assess muscle balance (quad:ham).
Limit
  • Limited specificity: sport isn't one speed.
Isotonic
What
  • Constant external resistance (bodyweight, dumbbells, barbells, machines).
  • Eccentric: ↑ force, ↓ energy cost → mechanotransduction → ↑ collagen synthesis.
Progress
  • Early slow → later faster, sport-specific.
Definitions
Terms
  • Neuromuscular control: respond to sensory feedback → joint stability.
  • Proprioception: input from skin, muscle, tendon, ligament, capsule receptors.
Post-injury deficit
Arthrogenic inhibition
  • Joint swelling → reflex inhibition of α-motor neuron → ↓ muscle activation.
Progress by altering
Variables
  • Surface stability: mini-trampoline, balance board, stability ball; squats/push-ups on unstable surface.
  • Vision (eyes closed). Speed ↑.
Treatment goal
Goal
  • Optimize tissue function; transition to play.
  • Progress repair exercises + add advanced, sport-specific work.
  • Progressive loading → ↑ collagen alignment + fiber hypertrophy.
Return to play
Criteria-based
  • ROM, strength, functional testing, patient-reported outcomes.
Pitfall
  • Less pain ≠ healed: pain ↓ before tissue healing completes.
Overdoing it
Risk
  • Athlete is tempted to do too much too soon → injured tissue still needs attention.
Functional specificity
Principle
  • Mimic activity demands: joint angle, velocity, closed chain, neuromuscular control.
  • General → sport-specific; match movement speed to sport.
Basketball guard (ankle sprain)
Progression
  • Single-joint general work → sport/position-specific.
  • Slow balance/strength → plyometrics → sprinting.
Sprinter (hamstring strain)
Progression
  • Flexibility → eccentric → concentric → dynamic stretch → rapid isotonic.
Closed kinetic chain
What
  • Terminal joint fixed/restrained; distal segment stationary.
  • e.g. squat, push-up.
Benefit
  • ↑ joint stability + function: joints work with adjacent joints/muscles.
Open kinetic chain
What
  • Terminal joint free to move.
  • e.g. leg extension, biceps curl, bench press.
Benefit
  • Isolates a joint/muscle (quads at knee).
Sport uses both
Example
  • Sprinting: one leg closed, other open.
So
  • Open chain can be equally appropriate.

Topic 05 — Program Design: Resistance Training
Three Rehab Protocols
Big picture
Core idea
  • DeLorme and Oxford: 3 × 10 pyramids.
  • DAPRE: auto-regulated.
DeLorme
Pattern
  • Light → heavy.
Oxford
Pattern
  • Heavy → light.
DAPRE
Full name
  • Daily adjustable progressive resistive exercise.
What it is
Design
  • 3 sets × 10 reps, pyramid design.
  • Resistance builds across sets.
How it works
Sets
  • Set 1: 10 reps @ 50% 10RM.
  • Set 2: 10 reps @ 75% 10RM.
  • Set 3: 10 reps @ 100% 10RM.
Implication
Benefit
  • Built-in warm-up from progressive increase.
What it is
Design
  • Reverse of DeLorme.
  • 3 sets × 10 reps.
How it works
Sets
  • Set 1: 100% 10RM.
  • Set 2: 75% 10RM.
  • Set 3: 50% 10RM.
Implication
Caution
  • No built-in warm-up → add a non-fatiguing warm-up set.
What it is
Design
  • 4 sets; reps 10 → as low as 1.
Edge
  • More control of intensity + volume than DeLorme/Oxford.
How it works
Sets
  • Set 1: 10 reps @ 50% est. 6RM.
  • Set 2: 6 reps @ 75%.
  • Set 3: max reps @ 100% est. 6RM.
Then
  • Set 3 reps → sets resistance for set 4.
Implication
Adjusts daily
  • Resistance adjusts to daily performance.

Topic 05 — Program Design: Resistance Training

From Protocol to Program

SAID Principle
System adapts to imposed demands → training goal dictates program design.
Protocol Limits
DeLorme/Oxford/DAPRE ↑ strength.
May be too strict to individualize for different sports.
Patellofemoral remodeling: marathoner → quads trained for muscular endurance (many reps). Weightlifter → fewer reps, high intensity for power.

Topic 05 — Program Design: Resistance Training
Patellofemoral Rehab by Sport
Inflammatory
Avoid
  • No quad work (relative rest).
Maintain
  • Hip extensors, knee flexors, plantar flexors: strength + endurance.
  • Cardiovascular fitness.
Fibroblastic
Quads
  • Isometric quads at full extension → multiple angles → pain-free isotonic.
  • 2–3 × 15–20 @ ≤ 50% 1RM.
Aerobic
  • Bike/stair stepper.
Maturation
Sport-specific
  • Gradual return to running (distance/speed).
  • Add lunge + squat (↑ knee ROM).
  • 2–3 × 15–20 @ 50–75% 1RM.
Inflammatory
Avoid
  • No quad work (relative rest).
Maintain
  • Adjacent areas: strength + power.
  • Upper-body strength + power.
Fibroblastic
Quads
  • Isometric quads at full extension → multiple angles → pain-free isotonic.
  • 3–4 × 8–10 @ ≤ 50% 1RM.
Power
  • Continue upper-body power.
Maturation
Sport-specific
  • Competition-like movement speeds.
  • Add Romanian deadlift + squat (↑ knee ROM).
  • 4–5 × 3–8 @ > 75% 1RM.

Topic 06 — Program Design: Aerobic & Anaerobic
Aerobic & Anaerobic Conditioning
Mimic the sport
Rule
  • No optimal rehab aerobic program established.
  • Mimic sport + metabolic demands as closely as possible.
Who
  • S&C professional = ideal to prescribe/supervise.
Respect the injury
Rule
  • Account for sport demands + injury contraindications.
  • Follow standard prescription guidelines → uncomplicated return.
Marathon runner
Priority
  • Aerobic fitness → address immediately.
Wrestler
Priority
  • Aerobic + anaerobic → interval training.
Weightlifter
Priority
  • Anaerobic fitness → maintain.
Same injury, different plan
Takeaway
  • Same patellofemoral injury, three different conditioning programs.
Modalities
Options
  • Upper-body ergometer, deep-water running, lower-extremity cycling, elliptical.
Choose
  • By injured region; upper-extremity work can ↑ O₂ consumption.
Start early
When
  • Even in inflammatory phase: minimize stress to healing tissue, apply stress to uninjured areas.
Uninjured limb
Example
  • Right-knee injury: upper body + left single-leg squat w/ weights.
Benefit
  • Training the uninjured limb ↑ strength in the involved limb.
Caution
  • Modify uninjured-limb exercises to keep the involved limb protected.

Topic 07 — Reducing Risk of Injury & Reinjury
Reducing Reinjury Risk
Upper extremity
Risk factors
  • ↓ glenohumeral ROM, scapular dyskinesis, ↓ shoulder strength.
  • Overhead athletes: ↓ shoulder IR ROM → shoulder injury; ↓ ER/flexion ROM → elbow injury.
Lower extremity
Risk factors
  • ↓ balance, ↓ neuromuscular control in landing, ↓ muscle strength.
Previous injury
Top risk
  • One of the most substantial risk factors for future injury.
ROM + Throwers Ten
Program
  • ROM exercises + Throwers Ten.
Shoulder ER strengthening
Program
  • Shoulder external-rotation strengthening.
Sleeper stretch
Effect
  • ↑ IR, ↓ posterior tightness.
Sport-specific work
Program
  • Neuromuscular control in landing + cutting.
Sportsmetrics / PEP
Effect
  • ↓ ACL injuries + ankle sprains.
Jump/landing technique
Program
  • Jump/landing technique + single-leg squat.
Eccentric hamstring work
Effect
  • Eccentric exercise → dramatically ↓ hamstring injury.
Residual deficits
Problem
  • Strength, biomechanics, functional performance may lag.
Check
  • Compare vs contralateral limb or normative values.
Acceptable gap
Target
  • Side-to-side difference < 10% in strength + functional performance.
Handoff
Critical
  • Transition from supervised rehab → unrestricted play.
Team
  • Must communicate how deficits are managed.

Topic 08 — Medical Conditions
Medical Conditions
Four conditions
Why they matter
  • Conditions that can develop from training or pre-exist and raise exercise risk.
Rhabdomyolysis
One-liner
  • Muscle breakdown → myoglobin.
Sickle cell trait
One-liner
  • One abnormal hemoglobin gene.
Heat illness
One-liner
  • Cramps → syncope → exhaustion → heatstroke.
Cold exposure
One-liner
  • Hypothermia.
What it is
Definition
  • Skeletal muscle breakdown → myoglobin into blood → kidney damage/failure risk.
Triggers
  • Trauma, extreme exertion, muscle compression.
Signs
Presentation
  • Severe pain/weakness, swelling, tenderness; cola-colored urine (myoglobinuria).
  • Also fatigue, nausea, vomiting, confusion; severe: dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, acute kidney injury.
Response & prevention
If suspected
  • Stop activity, lie down, hydrate, monitor, refer promptly.
Prevent
  • Avoid excessive/unaccustomed intensity, volume, duration; consider baseline fitness.
What it is
Genetics
  • Inherited: 1 abnormal + 1 normal hemoglobin gene.
  • (Sickle cell disease = 2 abnormal genes.)
Trigger
  • Extreme exertion/low O₂ (altitude) → RBCs sickle + clump → vessel constriction.
Signs & risks
Presentation
  • Fatigue, pain, swelling of hands/feet, vision problems.
  • Long-term: vessel damage, ↓ RBC lifespan → anemia, stroke.
  • Linked to sudden death in extreme exertion.
Response & prevention
If symptoms
  • Stop, leave extreme temperature, hydrate, refer.
Prevent
  • Know triggers, SCT testing, medical follow-up, acclimatize, stay ≤ anaerobic threshold, active cool-down (lactate clearance).
Heat cramps
What
  • Involuntary sustained contraction of large muscle groups, during/after exercise in heat.
  • Causes: dehydration, electrolyte loss, ↑ load/duration, fatigue; core temp not always ↑.
Tx / prevent
  • Stop, cool, rehydrate, gentle passive stretch/massage.
  • Hydrate, light clothing, acclimatize.
Heat syncope
What
  • Dizziness/fainting during or right after training.
  • Risks: no acclimatization, dehydration, venous pooling, low BP.
Tx
  • Supine, legs above heart; vitals; shield from heat; oral rehydration.
  • Low BP/frequent syncope → medical consult.
The continuum
Key idea
  • Heat illness = continuum of thermoregulation failure.
  • Heatstroke is preceded by cramps, syncope, exhaustion.
Heat exhaustion
What
  • Can't continue exercise in heat: low BP, dehydration, heavy sweating, electrolyte loss.
  • Pallor, cramps, weakness, syncope, headache, nausea, dark/↓ urine; core temp up to 104.9 °F (40.5 °C).
Tx
  • Remove from heat, rehydrate (IV if needed), aggressive cooling; ice bath if ineffective.
Heatstroke
Medical emergency
  • Progression of exhaustion.
  • Rapid HR, hypotension, hyperventilation, altered mental state, seizure, coma.
  • Core temp > 109.4 °F (43 °C) linked to death.
Tx
  • Total-body ice immersion, monitor core temp, call EMS.
Prevention
Prevent
  • Acclimatize + hydrate before/during/after.
  • Catch cramps/exhaustion early.
What it is
Definition
  • Core temp < 95 °F (35 °C) → systems ↓ function → eventual shutdown.
  • Mild: manageable. Severe: medical emergency.
Signs & risks
Early signs
  • Shivering, pale dry skin, ↑ muscle tone; ↑ HR/BP/respiration (thermogenesis).
Risks
  • Cold without warming methods; rain/cold water → wet clothing → heat loss.
Response
Do
  • Warm body + environment; monitor temp.
  • < 89.6 °F (32 °C) → cardiovascular failure risk.
Note
  • Acclimatizes to heat; little/no acclimation to cold → recognize extremes, wear protective clothing.
